title: How Much to Tip at a Bar in NYC: Per Drink, Tabs and Tax
h1: How Much to Tip at a Bar in NYC (and How Happy Hour Changes the Math)
keyword: how much to tip at a bar in nyc
description: How much to tip at a bar in NYC: the per-drink and per-tab customs, the city sales tax, happy hour math, and tips for visitors new to tipping.
answer: How much to tip at a bar in NYC? NYC Tourism's guide puts the custom at a dollar or more per drink, or 18 to 20 percent when you pay a whole tab by card. Tipping is a custom, not a law, but it is a real part of bartenders' pay. At a happy hour such as Phebes in the East Village or The Wolfhound in Astoria, etiquette writers suggest tipping on the regular menu price, not the deal price.
intro:
Tipping is the part of a New York night out that confuses visitors most, and plenty of locals second-guess it too. There is no law that sets a bar tip. What exists is a strong custom, described in NYC Tourism's visitor guide and in etiquette advice from food and drink writers, plus a few legal facts that shape your bill: the city sales tax, and how service charges work.

This guide walks through the customs as they are usually described, then the math: per drink versus per tab, where tax fits, and what to do when the drinks are discounted. The five picks are happy hours on our list with a clear, itemized drink deal, spread across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx, so you can practice the math on a real menu.

picks.why: Phebes is an East Village pub on the Bowery with a short, itemized happy hour: beers, Guinness and Stella drafts, wines and select cocktails, each at its own deal price. It runs Monday through Friday from late afternoon into the evening, holidays excluded. A list this clear makes the tip math easy. Bleecker Street on the 6 and the B, D, F and M is a four-minute walk.

Winnie's is a cocktail bar on West 52nd Street in the Times Square area, with happy hour Tuesday through Friday into the evening. The list covers a light draft, select wine, an Aperol spritz, well mixed drinks and an espresso martini. Its posted prix-fixe menu notes that tax and gratuity are not included, a good reminder to read the fine print. The 1 at 50th Street is a two-minute walk.

Pete's Candy Store on Lorimer Street keeps its happy hour simple: draft beer, well drinks and wines share one deal price, with Athletic Upside Dawn cans listed too, Monday through Friday until early evening. Sandwiches and snacks such as a classic grilled cheese are on the menu. One price across the list makes a round easy to add up. Lorimer Street on the G and L is a six-minute walk.

The Wolfhound is an Astoria pub on 30th Avenue with a three-line happy hour: draught beer, mixed drinks and wine, all at the same deal price, on weekdays until early evening. That flat price makes it easy to tip either way, cash per drink as you go or a percentage when you close out. The 30th Avenue station on the N and W is an eight-minute walk.

Tin Marin Tapas Bar on Riverdale Avenue brings a clear deal to the Bronx. Happy hour runs Monday through Thursday from mid-afternoon into the evening and on Friday from early afternoon, with sangria and margaritas (flavors cost a little extra), house wines and all beers. The 1 at 238th Street is a seven-minute walk.

sections.h: If you come from a country without tipping
sections.body:
In much of the world, the price on the menu is what you pay. In New York, a bar tab usually has two more pieces: sales tax, which is the law, and the tip, which is custom. Nobody can legally make you tip a bartender, but NYC Tourism's guide says bartenders typically expect it. New York labor law lets employers count tips toward part of a tipped food and drink worker's minimum wage, so for the person behind the bar, tips are part of the paycheck, not a bonus.

There are exceptions. NYC Tourism notes that some places run a no-tipping policy and say so on the menu or bill, usually with a service or administrative charge or higher prices instead. Restaurants may also add a gratuity for larger groups. If you see a line labeled gratuity or service charge, read it before you add more.

NYC Tourism describes two common ways to tip a bartender. Paying as you go, the custom is at least a dollar per drink, and more when the drinks are pricey, such as a craft cocktail. Running a tab on a card, the usual move is 18 to 20 percent of the total instead.

The two methods can land in different places. A dollar on a simple beer is a bigger share of the price than a dollar on a cocktail, so a percentage tends to be fairer on an expensive round, and per-drink cash tends to be generous on cheap beer. Pick one approach for the night and stick with it.

Food and drink served for on-premises consumption at bars and restaurants is taxable in New York State. In New York City, the combined sales tax rate is 8.875 percent, made up of 4.5 percent city tax, 4 percent state tax and a 0.375 percent Metropolitan Commuter Transportation District surcharge, according to the NYC Department of Finance. Voluntary tips you leave are not subject to sales tax, according to the state tax department.

For sit-down dining, NYC Tourism frames the standard tip as a share of the pre-tax bill. A quick check: double the tax line on your receipt and you get a little under 18 percent of the pre-tax total, the low end of the usual range. Round up from there.

sections.h: Happy hour math: full price or deal price?
sections.body:
This is where people disagree most. The common advice from etiquette writers, including a bartending etiquette piece in HuffPost and a guide from Food Republic, is to tip on the regular menu price, not the discounted one. The logic: the bartender makes the same drink and does the same work at the happy hour price. The HuffPost piece also suggests tipping on comped drinks.

If you do not know the regular price, Food Republic suggests tipping about 25 percent of the price you paid. Not everyone follows this, and nothing requires it. A fair middle ground is to tip at least what you would on a full-price round of the same drinks. Our pick cards show live happy hour prices, so you can see how far the deal moves the bill.

If you pay by card, the screen will usually ask about the tip. NYC Tourism notes that card terminals usually offer preset choices, often 15, 18 or 20 percent, along with a custom amount or no tip. The presets are suggestions, so choose what fits the service.

Cash still works well for per-drink tips, especially at a crowded bar where you order one round at a time. If you open a tab, you tip once when you close out, which keeps things simple for a group. Before you sign, check the bill for a service charge or an added gratuity, so you do not tip twice by accident.

faq.a: No. Tipping a bartender is a custom, not a legal requirement. A gratuity or service charge printed on your bill is part of what you owe, though, so read the bill before you add more.
faq.q: Is tipping at a bar required by law in New York City?

faq.a: NYC Tourism's guide describes the custom as at least a dollar per drink, and more when the drinks are expensive. On a card tab, it suggests 18 to 20 percent of the total instead.
faq.q: How much should I tip per drink in NYC?

faq.a: Common etiquette advice, from writers at HuffPost and Food Republic, is to tip on the regular menu price, since the work is the same. It is a custom, not a rule. If you do not know the regular price, Food Republic suggests about 25 percent of what you paid.
faq.q: Should I tip on the happy hour price or the full price?

faq.a: The combined sales tax rate in New York City is 8.875 percent, according to the NYC Department of Finance. Food and drink served at bars and restaurants is taxable.
faq.q: What is the sales tax on drinks at NYC bars?

faq.a: NYC Tourism frames the standard restaurant tip as a share of the pre-tax bill. Tipping on the total instead works out a little higher.
faq.q: Do I tip on the amount before or after tax?

faq.a: Yes. Card terminals usually show preset tip options, often 15, 18 or 20 percent, plus a custom amount. Cash per drink is the other common approach NYC Tourism describes.
faq.q: Can I tip on a card at an NYC bar?

title: Astoria Bar Crawl: 5 Happy Hours Around Ditmars
h1: Astoria bar crawl: five happy hours at the end of the N and W
description: An Astoria bar crawl with five weekday happy hours in walking order around Astoria–Ditmars Boulevard, plus trivia nights and the N and W from Manhattan.
answer: For an Astoria bar crawl, go Monday through Friday and stay close to the last stop of the N and W: Sweet Spot Sporting Lounge & Bar on 31st Street, then Burgerology Astoria, Rivercrest and The Ditty on Ditmars Boulevard, and a finish at The Bonnie on 23rd Avenue. All five run happy hour on those days, and the whole loop is under a kilometer, about ten minutes of walking.
intro:
Astoria suits a short crawl. The bars around Astoria–Ditmars Boulevard, the last stop on the N and W, sit within a few blocks of the station, so the evening goes to drinking rather than walking. This route covers five of them in a loop: one stop on 31st Street, three in a row on Ditmars Boulevard, and a finish on 23rd Avenue, about 830 meters in all.

The five happy hours overlap Monday through Friday, in the late afternoon and early evening. Sweet Spot opens its window first, so that is where you start, with a happy hour food menu to build a base. Burgerology adds sliders. Then the drinks take over: cocktails on tap at Rivercrest, classic cocktails at The Ditty, and The Bonnie, which also runs a late-night happy hour, so the last stop can turn into the rest of the night.

The cards below show live prices and today's hours for each stop. The table further down lists every happy hour within about 700 meters of the route, which helps when one bar is full and you need a swap.

picks.why: Start one minute from the station at Sweet Spot Sporting Lounge & Bar, 22-72 31st Street. Its weekday happy hour opens before any other on this route, which is why it goes first. The food list is the longest of the night: quesadillas, a classic burger, fish tacos, boneless wings, hot dogs and nachos, plus set-price beers and shots. The bar notes that items change with availability, so check the board when you arrive.

About four minutes east, Burgerology Astoria sits at 3129 Ditmars Boulevard. Its happy hour runs Monday through Friday and is served only at the bar, so aim for stools rather than a table. Well cocktails, wine and select drafts are on it, along with sliders in three styles (the house version, short rib and buffalo chicken) and a turkey burger. The menu says other cocktails and beers get a smaller discount too.

Rivercrest is a one-minute walk farther along Ditmars Boulevard, at 33-15. Its weekday happy hour starts when the doors open and ends in the early evening, and it covers drafts, wine and the specialty cocktails the bar pours on tap, a margarita among them. No food is listed on the happy hour, which is why the two eating stops come first. There is no booking link, so walk in.

The Ditty is practically next door at 35-03 Ditmars Boulevard, less than a minute from Rivercrest. It is the only stop on the route with an afternoon happy hour every day, weekends included. The list covers classic cocktails such as the Old Fashioned, Negroni, Paloma and Daiquiri, spirits with any mixer, Narragansett, and white, rosé, red and sparkling wine. NYC Trivia League runs music bingo here every other Monday.

Walk back west about five minutes, past the station, to The Bonnie at 29-12 23rd Avenue. Its happy hour runs Monday through Thursday from late afternoon, Friday from midday, and again late every night, so this is the stop to settle into. The early deal takes money off select draft beer, wine and well drinks, and the late one adds an espresso martini, a spicy margarita or a beer and a shot. NYC Trivia League hosts trivia here on Tuesdays, and Resy takes bookings.

sections.h: The route and when it works
sections.body:
Go Monday through Friday. Those are the days all five stops list a happy hour, and the windows overlap from the late afternoon into the early evening. The weekend is a different story. The Ditty is the only stop with an afternoon happy hour on Saturday and Sunday, and Rice K, a few doors from The Bonnie on 23rd Avenue, lists one daily as well, so those two make a short weekend pair, with The Bonnie's late-night window to finish.

The legs are short. Sweet Spot to Burgerology is about 290 meters, four minutes east toward Ditmars Boulevard. Burgerology to Rivercrest is about 80 meters, one minute. Rivercrest to The Ditty is about 40 meters on the same stretch of the boulevard. The Ditty to The Bonnie is the longest leg, about 420 meters and five minutes, back west past the station to 23rd Avenue. The total is roughly 830 meters and ten minutes, measured in straight lines between doors, so the real walk runs a little longer.

Most of these windows close together in the early evening, so plan on about half an hour per stop and keep the middle three moving. The Bonnie is the one place where the clock matters less, since its second happy hour comes back late in the night.

sections.h: Getting there on the N and W
sections.body:
Both lines end at Astoria–Ditmars Boulevard, and the MTA's station list marks it as the last stop, so you cannot ride past it. From Manhattan, the N and W both stop at 14 St-Union Sq, 34 St-Herald Sq, Times Sq-42 St, 57 St-7 Av and Lexington Av/59 St, then cross into Queens at Queensboro Plaza and run up through Astoria on elevated tracks. The W also makes local stops in Manhattan that the N skips, such as 23 St and 8 St-NYU.

The MTA timetable says the W runs on weekdays only, while the N runs at all times. That suits this crawl, which is a weekday plan anyway, but for a weekend pair at The Ditty and Rice K, or for the ride home late at night, count on the N.

One thing to know before you go: the MTA's station data lists Astoria–Ditmars Boulevard as not accessible. If you need an elevator, use Astoria Boulevard, one stop south on the same lines, which is listed as accessible. Sweet Spot is about eight minutes on foot from there.

Eat at the first two stops. Sweet Spot's happy hour food runs from a grilled chicken quesadilla and a Santa Fe wrap to a crispy chicken sandwich with fries, a classic burger, fried fish tacos, boneless wings, hot dogs and nachos supreme. Burgerology follows with its sliders and a turkey burger, served at the bar.

After that, the happy hour lists are drinks only. Rivercrest and The Ditty list no food, and The Bonnie, which describes itself as a cocktails and bar food spot, lists drinks only on its happy hour. If you get hungry again later, Rice K on 23rd Avenue carries a food-deal tag and says its daily happy hour includes appetizers.

You can pick your day by the game. On Tuesday, finish at The Bonnie, where NYC Trivia League lists a weekly trivia night that starts after the happy hour ends. On Thursday, The Bier & Cheese Collective, a few steps from The Ditty at 35-11 Ditmars Boulevard, has weekly trivia from the same league, and SingleCut Beersmiths, about nine minutes northeast at 19-33 37th Street, runs music bingo. SingleCut has trivia on Fridays too. On Monday, The Ditty hosts music bingo every other week, so confirm with the bar first. On Sunday there is trivia at Mosaic on 24th Avenue, about five minutes west of The Bonnie. Farther south in Astoria there are more games: trivia at Sunswick 35/35 on Wednesday, trivia on Monday and music bingo on Thursday at Oliver's Astoria on Broadway, and trivia at Bar Dalia on 31st Avenue on Sunday. Our Queens trivia page lists every game in the borough by night, and the music bingo page covers bingo across the city.

Only The Bonnie lists a booking link, on Resy. The other four have none, so plan on walking in. A group of two to four moves along Ditmars Boulevard far more easily than a big party, especially at Burgerology, where the happy hour is served at the bar only. If you are coming from Manhattan, treat the ride as part of the plan and arrive early enough to catch Sweet Spot's window; the cards show today's hours. Tip as you would anywhere in the city, and our guide to tipping at NYC bars covers how much. For another night in the neighborhood, the Astoria happy hours page also covers the 30th Avenue and Broadway clusters, which have enough bars for a second crawl.

faq.a: Monday through Friday, when all five stops list a happy hour and the windows overlap in the late afternoon and early evening. On weekends only The Ditty and Rice K have afternoon happy hours, and The Bonnie adds its late-night one.
faq.q: What day should I do an Astoria bar crawl?

faq.a: About 830 meters in straight lines between the five doors, or roughly ten minutes of walking. The longest leg is The Ditty to The Bonnie at about five minutes; the others take one to four.
faq.q: How long is the walk?

faq.a: Take the N or W to Astoria–Ditmars Boulevard, the last stop. Both trains stop at Union Square, Herald Square, Times Square, 57th Street and Lexington Avenue/59th Street. The W runs on weekdays only and the N runs at all times.
faq.q: How do I get to Astoria from Manhattan for this crawl?

faq.a: Sweet Spot has a happy hour food menu with quesadillas, burgers, fish tacos, boneless wings, hot dogs and nachos, and Burgerology has sliders and a turkey burger at the bar. Rivercrest and The Ditty list drinks only.
faq.q: Where can I eat on the route?

faq.a: Yes. NYC Trivia League lists weekly trivia at The Bonnie on Tuesday and at The Bier & Cheese Collective on Thursday, music bingo at SingleCut Beersmiths on Thursday and trivia there on Friday, and music bingo at The Ditty every other Monday.
faq.q: Is there trivia near the route?

title: Where to Watch Football in NYC: 8 Bars With Happy Hours
h1: Where to watch football in NYC: game day bars and their deals
keyword: where to watch football in nyc
description: Where to watch football in NYC: eight bars in Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens whose own sites talk up game day, plus their happy hour days.
answer: If you are deciding where to watch football in NYC, start with bars that say so on their own websites. The Commissioner in Park Slope promises football Sundays, O'Flanagan's on the Upper East Side lists NFL Sunday Ticket, and The Dawson 39 near Bryant Park advertises wall-to-wall TVs to catch every game. Soccer fans should look at Tavern29, Meller's Sports Hub and Kent Ale House.
intro:
It is the middle of football season. College games fill Saturdays, the NFL takes over Sundays, and plenty of New Yorkers would rather watch with a room full of fans than alone on the couch. The catch is that a sports bar sign does not tell you which game will be on the screen near your stool, or whether the bar carries the package your out-of-town team needs.

So we built this list a different way. Every bar here is tagged as a sports bar or a pub in our data, and for six of the eight we read the bar's own website and found it saying, in its own words, that it shows games: football Sundays, NFL Sunday Ticket, every soccer match or every game. The other two earn their spot with long happy hours, one of which reaches into the weekend, and we describe them only as far as their sites go. The picks are spread over Midtown, Union Square, the Upper East Side, Park Slope, Williamsburg and Astoria.

Each card shows the live happy hour days and prices. Most of these deals are weekday deals, so we point out the ones that reach Saturday or Sunday. For a big game, call ahead: what a website promised last season is not a promise for this weekend.

picks.why: An Irish restaurant and sports bar on West 39th Street, a short walk from Bryant Park. Its own site promises wall-to-wall HD TVs and tells you to catch every game, across two floors. Our listing has happy hour Monday through Friday from midday and all day on Saturday and Sunday, so a weekend game day can stay on the deal. 42nd Street-Bryant Park on the 7, B, D, F and M is two minutes away.

A pub on East 29th Street, a minute from the 28th Street station on the 6. Its site says it shows all soccer games, from the Premier League and Champions League to La Liga, and all college sports league games, and it keeps a separate game day menu. Happy hour runs on weekdays from lunch into the evening and covers an IPA, a Negroni and a Rose Hill sangria, which makes it a strong pick for a midweek match.

A pub on Waverly Place near Washington Square Park, two minutes from 8th Street-NYU on the R and W. Its site lists 14 HD TVs, plus pool and darts. The happy hour runs Monday through Friday, from the afternoon into the early evening, with buffalo wings on the list. That makes it a weekday pick for an early kickoff or a midweek match.

A pub on First Avenue on the Upper East Side, tagged as a sports bar in our data. Its website lists NFL Sunday Ticket and Fox Soccer Plus among the sports it shows, though parts of that page look several seasons old, so call to confirm before kickoff. Happy hour is a weekday deal that runs into the early evening, with well drinks on the list. The 72nd Street Q station is about seven minutes on foot.

A family-owned sports bar on Second Avenue. Its site counts more than 25 TVs, including private booths with their own screens, and calls itself a home for Premier League and European soccer, with Arsenal fans welcome for every match. The happy hour is a late one, Sunday through Thursday, covering wine, mixed and frozen drinks, margaritas and Aperol, so it fits the end of a long Sunday. The 86th Street Q is two minutes away.

A neighborhood bar on Fifth Avenue in Park Slope that calls itself a second living room and promises an exciting football Sunday on its own site. Happy hour runs Monday through Thursday until early evening, with money off all drafts and a set price on wine, well drinks and a beer and shot. So the deal is for after-work rounds; on Sunday you come for the crowd. Union Street on the R is four minutes away.

A pub on Kent Avenue in Williamsburg whose site describes it as a sports and craft beer bar for watching rugby and soccer, with 11 TVs and 24 taps. Happy hour runs Monday to Friday into the early evening, and the listed deal is a seltzer and shot pairing. Soccer and rugby come first here, so ask before you count on an American football game. Bedford Avenue on the L is about seven minutes on foot.

A pub on 31st Street in Astoria, a minute from the Broadway station on the N and W. Its site pitches it as a place to watch the big game or meet up with friends. Daly's has one of the longest happy hour windows on this list: every day of the week, weekends included, from late morning into the evening, so a Saturday or Sunday afternoon there stays on happy hour prices for hours.

sections.h: Sunday game day and weekend happy hours
sections.body: Here is the honest problem with football and happy hour in New York: most deals on our list run on weekdays, and the games you care about are mostly on weekends. A few of these picks bridge the gap. Daly's runs its happy hour every day, Saturday and Sunday included. The Dawson 39 is listed Monday through Friday from midday and all day on Saturday and Sunday, and Meller's runs a late deal from Sunday through Thursday. For more options by day, browse Saturday happy hours, Sunday happy hours or the full weekend list, and our weekend happy hours guide. Plan around kickoff. On the official Giants and Jets schedules, many of this season's Sunday home games are listed for 1 p.m. Eastern, with the odd prime-time game mixed in, such as a Thursday night home game for the Giants in November. If your game is in that early Sunday window, a bar whose deal runs all afternoon, like The Dawson 39 or Daly's, keeps the second and third rounds on happy hour prices. For a late game, our guide to what time bars close in NYC explains the rules.

sections.h: How to pick a bar for your team
sections.body: Ask ahead. A message or a call the day before is the simplest way to find out whether your game will be on, which screen it will be on and whether the sound will be up. If your team is not a local one, ask whether the bar carries NFL Sunday Ticket; O'Flanagan's lists it on its site. Soccer fans should ask which league gets priority when matches overlap, since Tavern29, Meller's and Kent Ale House all lean toward soccer. Arrive early. The tables with a clear view go first, especially when a New York team plays or a big rivalry is on. Groups should ask whether the bar takes reservations for game days, and pay attention to any minimums. Tip like you plan to stay for four quarters; our guide on how much to tip at a bar in NYC covers the norms. For more rooms with screens, see sports bar happy hours and pub happy hours, and for halftime entertainment try bars with games such as pool and darts.

The deals at the eight picks above are mostly about drinks, so if you want wings and fries on the discount too, look a little further. The Malt House in Greenwich Village runs its happy hour only on Saturday and Sunday, and the list includes jumbo wings and parmesan herbed fries. Third Avenue Ale House on the Upper East Side has a weekend afternoon happy hour that includes food, and its site describes a billiards room with large TV screens where you can come along to watch a game. For more, the happy hour food page lists every deal with food on it, and our cheap happy hour food guide picks out the ones worth building a meal around. Eating early in the game also keeps a long Sunday under control.

sections.h: Getting to MetLife Stadium from the city
sections.body: Both the Giants and the Jets play their home games at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, according to their official schedules. If you have tickets, NJ Transit's Meadowlands page describes the main route: take an NJ Transit train from Penn Station New York, at 32nd Street between 7th and 8th Avenues, to Secaucus Junction, then transfer to the shuttle train to Meadowlands Rail Station, steps from the stadium. That special rail service runs for large events, and NJ Transit notes you need a ticket to board the train from the Meadowlands back to Secaucus. By bus, NJ Transit's page points to the Coach USA 351 Meadowlands Express from the Port Authority Bus Terminal. Check the service on game day before you leave. A drink near Penn Station first is easy to arrange; see our guide to drinks near Grand Central and Penn Station.

faq.a: Start with bars that say so on their own sites. The Commissioner in Park Slope promises football Sundays, O'Flanagan's on the Upper East Side lists NFL Sunday Ticket, and The Dawson 39 near Bryant Park says you can catch every game. Call ahead to confirm your game.
faq.q: Where can I watch NFL games in NYC?

faq.a: Of the bars on this list, O'Flanagan's on First Avenue lists NFL Sunday Ticket on its website. Parts of that page look dated, so call before Sunday to check that it is still offered this season.
faq.q: Which NYC bars have NFL Sunday Ticket?

faq.a: Tavern29 near the 28th Street 6 station says it shows all soccer games, Meller's Sports Hub on the Upper East Side calls itself a home for the Premier League, and Kent Ale House in Williamsburg is set up for soccer and rugby.
faq.q: Where can I watch soccer and the Premier League in NYC?

faq.a: Yes. The Dawson 39 near Bryant Park runs happy hour all day on Sunday, Daly's Pub in Astoria runs it every day, Sunday included, and Meller's has a late happy hour starting on Sunday. Check each card for the current window.
faq.q: Do any football bars have a happy hour on Sunday?

faq.a: Both teams play home games at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, according to the official Giants and Jets schedules.
faq.q: Where do the Giants and Jets play?

faq.a: For large events, NJ Transit runs trains from Penn Station New York to Secaucus Junction with a shuttle train on to Meadowlands Rail Station. NJ Transit's page also points to the Coach USA 351 Meadowlands Express from the Port Authority Bus Terminal.
faq.q: How do I get to MetLife Stadium from Manhattan?

method: We started from bars tagged as sports bars or pubs in our data and favored those with a weekend happy hour. On October 17, 2026 we read each candidate's own website and only say a bar shows games when that site says so; the other picks are described from our listings. title: Team Happy Hour NYC: 8 Bookable Spots Near the Office
h1: Team happy hour NYC: where to take your coworkers
description: Team happy hour NYC guide: eight bookable spots in FiDi, Flatiron, Midtown and Hudson Yards with drink and food deals, group space and bill tips.
answer: The simplest team happy hour NYC plan is a place that takes reservations and puts food on the deal: Lucky Tiger in the Financial District, Boqueria in Flatiron, Tara Mór and Legasea near Penn Station, and Take Care and Hofbräu Bierhaus near Grand Central. Every pick's own website says it hosts groups or private events, so you can ask for a room once the team outgrows the bar.
intro:
Getting ten coworkers into one bar after work is a different job from meeting a friend for a drink. You need space for everyone, a deal that covers food as well as drinks, and a location near the trains people take home. Plenty of office-district bars run a happy hour; fewer take a group booking.

This guide picks eight places in the Financial District, Flatiron, the blocks around Penn Station, Hudson Yards and Grand Central. Each runs a weekday happy hour with drinks and food, and we checked each venue's own website for group dining, private rooms or event space. Six list online reservations with us; Hofbräu Bierhaus takes smaller parties online through its own site, and Kyma takes group requests through its events page.

Below the picks: planning tips, a district view, a trivia alternative and how the bill works. Cards show live hours and prices.

picks.why: An Asian fusion restaurant on Pearl Street with several bars under one roof. The weekday happy hour runs at Dragon Bar and Night Market and covers select cocktails, mocktails and wine, a Kirin and shochu shot combo, and food, including a platter sized for four to six people. Its private events page lists four themed spaces and corporate events. Whitehall Street on the 1, R and W is two minutes away.

A Spanish tapas restaurant on West 19th Street with a happy hour every day, longest on weekdays. Built for sharing: pan con tomate, croquetas, patatas bravas, a serrano ham grilled cheese and beef sliders, plus mini martinis, a mini espresso martini and Spanish beer. Boqueria's events page says the Flatiron location offers private dining, semi-private dinners and business receptions. The 23rd Street F and M is four minutes away.

A Mexican cantina on West 27th Street, inside the Innside by Meliá hotel, with a Tuesday to Friday happy hour served at the bar. It covers tacos, margaritas, palomas and sangria, house wines and Mexican draft beers. The cantina's site says it handles large private events and group dining for up to 100 guests. The 28th Street station on the 1 is two minutes away.

An Irish pub on West 30th Street near Penn Station and the Garden. The Monday to Friday happy hour pairs Aperol spritzes, a Midtown Mule, margaritas, house wine and draft beer with a food special: choose any two apps, shares, fries or sides. Its private events page offers semi-private and private parties with no room rental fee, including a mezzanine lounge for groups of 12 or more. The 28th Street 1 is two minutes away.

A bar and grill on Seventh Avenue at 36th Street, inside the Moxy Times Square. The Monday to Friday happy hour covers oysters, fries, beer, wine and martinis, and it is served at the bar only, so it suits a smaller team that is happy to stand together. Walk-ins are welcome. Its site promotes special events for intimate celebrations or boardroom-style gatherings. The 1, 2 and 3 at Penn Station are two minutes away.

The Hudson Yards branch of Kyma, a Greek restaurant on West 35th Street. The Tuesday to Friday happy hour pours house wines including rosé, sauvignon blanc, pinot noir and prosecco, beers such as Mythos and Lagunitas IPA, and a short list of bites: spanakopita, calamari and tuna taquitos. Kyma's Hudson Yards events page takes large-group dining requests for eight or more, plus private and semi-private events. The 7 at 34th Street and Hudson Yards is four minutes away.

A German beer hall on Third Avenue, three minutes from Grand Central. The happy hour runs Monday to Thursday in the bar area only, with half-liter Hofbräu beers, house wine, well drinks and discounted appetizers. Its party page says the large communal tables suit group outings, that it specializes in corporate events and that parties of 15 or fewer can reserve online. On Mondays it also hosts a weekly trivia night, according to NYC Trivia League.

A restaurant and bar in the Shelburne Sonesta hotel on Lexington Avenue in Murray Hill, about a six-minute walk from Grand Central. The Monday to Friday happy hour covers cocktails, martinis, select wines, select drafts and shareable appetizers, so a few plates can feed the table. Take Care's site says it is available for private events. The 33rd Street 6 is five minutes away, and reservations go through SevenRooms.

sections.h: How to plan a team happy hour
sections.body: Book early in the week and give the headcount. A small team can usually get a table at the start of the window; twenty people usually means a section or a room, which goes through the venue's events form, so start early. Ask one question before anything else: does the happy hour apply at a reserved table, or only at the bar? Many deals are bar-only. Legasea and El Lugar Cantina serve theirs at the bar, Hofbräu Bierhaus limits it to the bar area, and Lucky Tiger names the two bars where it runs. Croton Reservoir Tavern near Bryant Park serves its happy hour in a downstairs speakeasy that is also the room it books for private events, so ask what happens to the deal on a night the room is taken. Settle the bill plan before the first round: one tab on one card if the company pays, or ask about separate checks at the start. For spots near the trains, see happy hours near Grand Central and near Penn Station.

Downtown, Lucky Tiger is the group option on our list; browse Financial District happy hours for more. In Flatiron and NoMad, Boqueria and El Lugar Cantina both lean on food you can share across a long table, and the Flatiron and Chelsea pages list alternatives nearby. Around Penn Station, Tara Mór and Legasea sit a few blocks apart, with Kyma a short walk west in Hudson Yards. Near Grand Central, Hofbräu Bierhaus and Take Care cover the east side. Our guide to after-work drinks at Grand Central and Penn Station has more stops, early happy hours helps if the team can leave mid-afternoon, and the Midtown and food deal pages list the rest.

sections.h: Trivia or games instead of another round
sections.body: A team that wants something to do can plan around a quiz. Hofbräu Bierhaus hosts trivia on Mondays, a happy hour day there too. Mad Dog & Beans, also near Grand Central, has a Monday trivia night and a Monday to Thursday happy hour at the bar. Downtown, Sadie's on Fulton Street runs trivia on Tuesdays and a weekday happy hour. All three nights are listed as weekly by NYC Trivia League. Schedules change, so confirm with the bar and ask about team size limits. Our trivia nights page lists quizzes by day, and bars with games covers groups that would rather play. See Hofbräu Bierhaus, Mad Dog & Beans and Sadie's for their current deals.

sections.h: The bill: tax, tips and group service charges
sections.body: Sales tax is added to food and drink served for on-premises consumption at bars and restaurants, according to the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, so the total will be higher than the menu prices. NYC Tourism also notes that many restaurants automatically add a gratuity for large parties, usually six or more. Check the bill before you add a tip so the group does not tip twice. The label on that line matters. The state tax department says voluntary tips are not subject to sales tax, and a mandatory gratuity is not taxed only if it is shown separately, identified as a tip or gratuity, and paid in full to the staff. A line called a service charge is taxable. For how much to leave, see how much to tip at a bar in NYC.

faq.a: Often, yes. Six of the eight picks list online reservations, Hofbräu Bierhaus says parties of 15 or fewer can book online, and Kyma takes large-group requests through its events page. Bigger groups should use the events form.
faq.q: Can you reserve a table for happy hour in NYC?

faq.a: Not always. Legasea and El Lugar Cantina serve their deals at the bar, Hofbräu Bierhaus limits it to the bar area, and Lucky Tiger names the bars where it runs. Ask when you book.
faq.q: Does the happy hour price apply to a reserved group table?

faq.a: Tara Mór on West 30th Street offers semi-private and private parties with no room rental fee, and Legasea on Seventh Avenue runs a bar happy hour with oysters and martinis.
faq.q: Where can a work team get happy hour near Penn Station?

faq.a: Hofbräu Bierhaus on Third Avenue has communal tables and books corporate events, with trivia on Mondays. Take Care on Lexington Avenue has weekday drinks and shareable appetizers and is available for private events.
faq.q: Where can coworkers go for happy hour near Grand Central?

faq.a: Many do. NYC Tourism says many restaurants add a gratuity for large parties, usually six or more. Read the bill before tipping.
faq.q: Will a restaurant add a tip automatically for a group?

method: Picks come from our list of NYC bars: we looked for weekday happy hours in office districts whose deal covers both drinks and food, preferring places that list reservations. title: Lower East Side Bar Crawl: 5 Happy Hours Near Orchard St
h1: Lower East Side bar crawl: five happy hours around Orchard Street
description: A Lower East Side bar crawl built on happy hours that overlap Monday to Friday: five stops from Hair Of The Dog to Boho Karaoke, about a kilometer on foot.
answer: For a Lower East Side bar crawl, go Monday through Friday and walk five stops in this order: Hair Of The Dog and Isla & Co. on Orchard Street, Ten Bells on Broome Street, Tre on Ludlow Street, then Boho Karaoke Orchard back on Orchard. All five run a happy hour on those days, they overlap in the late afternoon, and the whole walk is about a kilometer.
intro:
The Lower East Side packs a lot of bars into a few short blocks, and Orchard Street alone has four of the happy hours on our list within a couple of minutes of each other. That makes it an easy place to string a crawl together, as long as you pick bars whose deals are on at the same time. This route does that with five stops on Orchard, Broome and Ludlow Streets, and about 13 minutes of walking in total.

The order follows the clock as much as the map. You get a sports pub, a cafe bar, a natural wine bar with oysters, a restaurant wine stop and a karaoke finish.

Each card below shows live prices and today's hours. The table under this intro lists more happy hours within a short walk, in case a stop is packed.

picks.why: Start at Hair Of The Dog, a sports pub at 168 Orchard Street. Its weekday happy hour begins at midday, earlier than anything else on this route, and takes a discount off all drinks, with a slider deal alongside; the bar notes that exclusions apply. Order a slider here, since only one other stop lists food. The F at 2nd Avenue is three minutes away, and no booking link is listed, so walk in.

Walk two minutes south on Orchard to Isla & Co., a cafe and bar at 139 Orchard Street that takes its cue from Australian coffee culture. The happy hour runs every day and covers select cocktails, wines and beers. It has the shortest window of the five and ends first, which is why it comes second. Resy takes bookings, and Delancey Street station on the F, J, M and Z is three minutes away.

Ten Bells, a natural wine bar at 247 Broome Street, is about three minutes south of Isla & Co. Its happy hour starts when the doors open, every day of the week, and on weekdays that is late in the afternoon. The deal is oysters and a carafe of wine, so this is the seafood stop and a good place to share a carafe. Resy takes reservations, and Delancey Street station is two minutes away.

Head about six minutes north up Ludlow Street to Tre, a restaurant at 173 Ludlow. Its happy hour pours white wine, red wine, Champagne and Aperol, and it runs Monday through Friday in the early evening, with a longer window on weekends. On Thursdays the happy hour is served at the bar only, so take a seat there. The F at 2nd Avenue is three minutes away.

Finish at Boho Karaoke Orchard, 152 Orchard Street, two minutes back toward Delancey. Its happy hour runs every day from opening and stays on far longer than any other stop here. The list covers shots of lemon drop, kamikaze, sake or soju, plus draft beer, wine, cocktails and sake or soju bombs. Private karaoke rooms are available, so a group can end the night singing. Delancey Street station is three minutes away.

sections.body:
Go Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday or Friday. Those are the days all five happy hours run. All five are on together for a stretch in the late afternoon, and that shared window is your crawl.

Timing matters most at the start. Hair Of The Dog starts earliest. Isla & Co. ends first, and Ten Bells only opens in the late afternoon on weekdays, so reach Isla & Co. early in its window and move to Ten Bells as it opens. Ten Bells and Tre end at the same moment, so keep stops three and four to about half an hour each. Then the pressure is off: Boho Karaoke Orchard keeps its deal going into the evening.

On a Saturday, Hair Of The Dog drops out because its happy hour is weekdays only. A four-stop version still works: start at Tre, which has a longer weekend window, then Isla & Co., then Ten Bells, which opens earlier on Saturdays, and finish at Boho Karaoke Orchard. Ten Bells to Boho is about 330 meters, roughly four minutes.

Leg one, Hair Of The Dog to Isla & Co.: about 170 meters, two minutes, south on Orchard Street. Leg two, Isla & Co. to Ten Bells: about 235 meters, three minutes, continuing south on Orchard past Delancey Street to Broome Street. Leg three, Ten Bells to Tre: about 475 meters, six minutes, north up Ludlow Street. This is the longest walk of the night and a good moment to drink some water. Leg four, Tre to Boho Karaoke Orchard: about 150 meters, two minutes, one block over to Orchard Street. That adds up to roughly 1,025 meters and 13 minutes on foot. These are straight lines between map coordinates, so the street grid adds a little. If a stop is full, Mary's and Gugu Room are about a minute from Isla & Co., and Sally Can Wait is across Broome Street from Ten Bells. Their days differ, so check the table first, or see all Lower East Side happy hours.

sections.h: Getting there, getting home and what to bring
sections.body: Arrive on the F at 2nd Avenue, three minutes from Hair Of The Dog. Tre is three minutes from the same station if you join late. The rest of the route sits near Delancey Street station on the F, J, M and Z: Ten Bells is two minutes away, and Isla & Co. and Boho Karaoke Orchard are three, so the last stop leaves you close to four lines home. Bring ID. You must be 21 to be served in New York, and the State Liquor Authority holds the bar responsible even if a guest looked older. The ID it lists as acceptable is a valid driver's license from any U.S. state or Canada, a New York non-driver ID card, U.S. military ID, or a valid passport. College IDs do not count as the main proof of age. Visitors from outside the U.S. and Canada should carry a passport. Plan on tax and tip on top of the happy hour prices. NYC Tourism notes that listed prices usually do not include sales tax and that bartenders typically expect a tip for every drink they serve. Our guide on how much to tip at a bar in NYC covers how to tip on discounted drinks.

Only two stops list food in their happy hour, and both come early: the slider deal at Hair Of The Dog and oysters at Ten Bells. Eat at both. Isla & Co., Tre and Boho Karaoke Orchard list drinks only, so the second half of the night runs on what you ate in the first. For a sit-down meal, Ten Bells and Isla & Co. both take reservations through Resy. Our oyster happy hours page lists more places pairing oysters with a drink deal.

sections.h: After the crawl: trivia and parties
sections.body: On a Tuesday, you can loop back to the start. Hair Of The Dog hosts a weekly trivia night on Tuesday evenings, run by NYC Trivia League, and it begins after the happy hour ends. On Thursdays, NYC Trivia League also runs trivia at Sadie's Ward, 121 Essex Street, about a minute from Isla & Co. See Tuesday trivia in NYC or trivia in Manhattan for the rest of the week. On a Friday, the night can keep going on the same blocks. Reggaeton Fridays by reggaetonLABS is on October 23 at The Delancey, 168 Delancey Street, with an upscale casual dress code. For Halloween, DO NOT DISTURB at Hotel Chantelle fills three floors at 92 Ludlow Street on Friday, October 30, and on Saturday, October 31, Halloween at Pianos at 158 Ludlow Street, steps from Tre, has DJs in three rooms and a costume contest. All three are 21 and over. Browse Halloween parties or the full NYC parties list for more.

faq.a: Monday through Friday. All five stops on this route run a happy hour on those days, and they overlap in the late afternoon. On Saturdays, drop Hair Of The Dog and start at Tre.
faq.q: What day should I do a Lower East Side bar crawl?

faq.a: About 1,025 meters in straight lines between the five stops, or roughly 13 minutes of walking in total. The longest leg, Ten Bells to Tre, is about six minutes.
faq.q: How long is the walk?

faq.a: Hair Of The Dog includes a slider deal in its happy hour, and Ten Bells has oysters. Both come early in the route. Isla & Co., Tre and Boho Karaoke Orchard list drinks only in their happy hours.
faq.q: Where can I eat on this crawl?

faq.a: Arrive on the F at 2nd Avenue, three minutes from Hair Of The Dog. Leave from Delancey Street on the F, J, M or Z, three minutes from Boho Karaoke Orchard.
faq.q: Which subway should I take?

faq.a: Yes. Hair Of The Dog hosts NYC Trivia League trivia on Tuesday evenings, and Sadie's Ward at 121 Essex Street has NYC Trivia League trivia on Thursdays. Confirm with the venue before you go.
faq.q: Is there trivia near the route?

faq.a: You must be 21. The State Liquor Authority lists a valid U.S. or Canadian driver's license, a New York non-driver ID, U.S. military ID, or a valid passport. College IDs are not accepted as the main proof of age.
faq.q: What ID do bars on the Lower East Side accept?

method: Stops, deals, days, addresses, booking links and subway walking times come from each bar's own website as recorded in our database, with happy hours last checked between September 2 and October 17, 2026. On October 17, 2026 we also read the websites of Hair Of The Dog, Isla & Co., Ten Bells, Tre and Boho Karaoke Orchard for opening hours and day patterns. Parties come from our published party listings. ID rules come from the New York State Liquor Authority and the tax and tipping notes from NYC Tourism.
